### Review: approving the versions

A version into `release` is the paper on the evidence so far: approve it when what it claims is correct, supported by its evidence and readable as a paper, with no `must` finding on what it presents; work the study is still doing is no finding against it, and your record says what is still to come. A version into `final` is the delivery: approve it when it meets the objective and the venue would accept it. A record qualifying that judgement is no approval. Inspect each version `paper-repo` offers at its head, with the document the system built from that head (its `built-from` says which); when it is supported, push a review record to your own repository (the version, your review, your conclusion), then approve the pull request, and review again after a push to it. Never approve an empty delivery: the system does not check it, you do.

Read the document the system built from the version's head from its first page as the venue's reader: whether the abstract and introduction say what the paper claims and why it matters, whether each figure, table and experiment in the main text serves a claim, and whether it reads as a paper or as a record of the study (who did what, what was checked, a caveat repeated wherever a number appears). Judge as the venue's reviewers will from the first version you review: whether the argument holds, what it contributes, and whether its writing and presentation meet the standard of a paper the venue accepts, for a reader outside the study. `venue-repo` records how the venue's accepted papers write an abstract and an introduction and what figures and tables their main text holds: judge the version's writing and presentation against that record. Before you approve, your record names the strongest objections they would raise (novelty, the test the main claim rests on, baselines, certainty of the numbers, readability) and the work or evidence that answers each; narrowing a claim, labelling the weakness, or noting that the objective permits the result answers none. Check that the references cover the work a reviewer would expect cited and compared. Do not repeat a passed check on unchanged content: the document's `built-from` already ties it to its commit, so the record is about the research, not a proof that files are unchanged.

Mark each finding `must` or `may`. `must` is what the objective or the venue's recorded requirements demand, an error, a claim the evidence does not support, writing or presentation the venue's reviewers would mark down (an abstract or introduction a reader outside the study cannot follow on first reading among them), or an objection above the version does not answer (in a `release` version, one the study's remaining work will answer is recorded as such, not marked `must`); `may` is any other improvement, and its owner decides. A `must` says what would answer it with the world's resources. A finding keeps its mark across versions while its subject is unchanged. Open `may` findings do not hold a version back. Sort the readers' findings the same way.

When the version is not supported, request changes on the pull request and say every finding still open that can be acted on at that commit, not one per round. A finding for another role also goes to it, by an issue or through a neighbor. Judge a `final` version against the objective: every requirement and every finding the task points to is addressed with evidence; a `release` version, against what it claims. Only a result the supplied inputs cannot yield, shown by an attempt, is a limitation, stated in the paper and holding no version back; work that needs implementation, a tool, a stronger baseline, another test, or a setup the method normally generates is a finding.

# Deviations from / interpretations of the Brief (idea-repo `Brief`; started at rev 3 (2026-11-25 16:08 UTC); the thresholds in rev 4 (commit c6be9ad, wiki) are the ones the final runs record)

Each is logged when made; the paper must state them.

1. **Target set.** The Brief asks that R = P \ S be identical for every selector, which is impossible when S differs by selector. Primary design
   (`design=fixed`): a fixed target set T (30% of the columns, drawn at random, 5 partitions per fold) is held out; S is chosen among the other 70%;
   T is identical for every selector, predictor and k. The evaluator's literal problem (R = P \ S, S chosen among all N columns) is run as a
   secondary design (`design=allrest`) with random and greedy A-optimal only, to quantify the effect of R depending on S.
2. **r_eff.** Rank chosen by inner 5-fold held-out log-likelihood on training rows; because the likelihood is flat near its maximum, the
   smallest rank within one standard error of the best is used (`r_eff`); the arg-max (`r_argmax`) is reported alongside. Rank grid 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,10,12,15,20,25 (<= N/3).
3. **Closure** C(k) is computed on mean *squared* standardised error (the theory's risk is a squared error); RMSE-based skill is also reported.
4. **MTEB time proxy.** First-commit date is bulk-dominated in the pinned clone (largest single commit holds ~61-63% of pool models), so
   the model's `release_date` from its `model_meta.json` (100% coverage in both pools) is used for the time-forward split; first-commit is kept as a column.
5. **MTEB pools** (two, not pooled with each other): `mteb_eng` = English-only tasks, de-duplicated, top-coverage tasks such that >= 120 models
   have all (124 models x 70 tasks); `mteb_multi` = all-language tasks with coverage >= 100 models, greedy deletion to a complete block (117 x 247).
   Both rules are fixed in `code/build_mteb_matrix.py` and `code/make_pools.py`.
6. **Grid** for k: 1..10 (the H2 primary grid, capped at N/2) plus 12, 15, 20, 30 (capped at min(N/2, 0.7 N)) for the k-curve/k*.
7. **Best simple predictor (Brief rev 4, 'k* for two predictors').** The candidate set is {one-factor offset, ridge, kNN (k=10), Ledoit-Wolf Gaussian conditioning},
   wider than the Brief's parenthetical (one-factor, ridge/PLS), because the headline k* is a minimum over predictors and a wider set is the harder test for the
   PPCA method. The choice is made per outer fold on its TRAINING rows only (`code/best_simple.py`: inner grouped 5-fold, greedy-A selection, grid-averaged inner
   squared error); the held-out rows of the fold are not used. The same per-fold choice is applied to the random-selector errors. Soft-Impute is not in the set.
8. **Soft-Impute** is the 'fold-in' variant: lambda chosen on the training matrix (10% held-out cells), the shrinkage operator of the full training SVD is kept fixed and
   the new row is completed by the fixed point of x_T = [P x]_T given x_S. It is not a refit of the full matrix per new model. Compared in a paired run with 50 draws.
9. **Transform (C7).** Identity vs logit chosen per dataset on training folds by held-out log-likelihood *in original score space* (Jacobian included; `code/transform_choice.py`):
   logit is applied only to columns whose scores all lie strictly in (0,1) (clip 0.005); other columns stay identity. Primary criterion is the share of the 10 outer folds
   preferring the transform; held-out original-space error is the secondary criterion and is reported (they disagree on `mteb_multi`; the likelihood rule decides, as pre-stated).
   All main results use the chosen transform; the other one is a robustness row (`results/raw/robust`).
10. **Inner rank selection** uses random (not family-grouped) inner folds; siblings across inner folds may favour a larger rank slightly. The one-SE rule limits this; not changed.
11. **k* confidence intervals** are family-bootstrap percentiles of t

# Review of paper-repo#7 (main -> final), head 13c249e537a1

Document read: `document` branch, `main/document.pdf`, built-from 13c249e537a179f2e8e5b712371046b74a68cff7 (= head of main). 24 pages: main text 9 pages, references, appendices A-D, checklist.

## What the paper claims
Protocol (family-held-out, fit-before-select, paired family-clustered intervals) for "which k benchmarks to run on a new model"; factor model + greedy Bayesian A-optimal selection; on three dense blocks (MTEB-Eng 124x70, MTEB-Multi 117x247, HELM MMLU 79x57) k=3 closes 81-96% of the column-mean-to-LOBO gap, k*(0.9) = 1 (HELM MMLU) vs >=9 (MTEB, wide CIs); greedy beats random by 6-11% of error (mostly k<=3); later/stronger models predicted worse and too low; closed-form risk exact with known parameters, 36-69% off in level on real data; pre-specified H1 and H4 fail, H2 holds on one pool.

## Checked against code and results
Recomputed from `results/*.csv` (closure.csv, kstar.csv, gap.csv, paired_comparisons.csv, theory_gap.csv): C(3) 0.81/0.82/0.96; k* table incl. CIs and censoring shares; grid-averaged greedy-minus-random gaps and CIs (-0.038/-0.076/-0.044; 6.1/11.3/7.6%); per-k relative gaps (5-18% at k<=3, 1-5% at k=10, <3% at k=20); theory medians (0.5%, 26.7%->1.5%, 36/47/69%). All match the paper. `code/DEVIATIONS.md` and `code/RESULTS.md` agree with the paper's account of departures. The README maps every result file to a script, with pins, seeds, versions and run times. Negative and unexpected results (H1, H2 margin, H4, coherence argument, vacuous Chernoff, factor model no better than ridge) are reported as they fell. No fabricated number found.

## Strongest objections a reviewer would raise, and whether answered
1. **Setting and external validity (not answered) - must M1.** The task's setting is a leaderboard matrix with missing cells and a new model with a few measured entries. Every result is on dense blocks the study cut out (124 of 535 models x 70 of 567 tasks; 117 x 247 of 535 x 1256), which Table 1 shows differ from the rest (outside models larger, newer, 0.7-0.9 SD higher). The method and code already have a masked-EM variant (`bmk/fa.py`), yet it is never run on a sparse matrix; the history sweep only masks cells of a dense history while test models stay complete. Narrowing the claim to "the pool" (as the paper does) is honest but leaves the central question - does greedy selection + factor model work on the leaderboard as it is - unanswered. What would answer it: run the grouped protocol on the full sparse MTEB matrix (or on graded-density subsets, e.g. models/tasks with coverage >= 30/50/70%), with the factor model fitted by masked EM, candidate set = benchmarks observed for the test model, targets = a random 30% of its observed cells; report greedy A vs random vs column mean and the k-curve with family-clustered intervals, and say how closure is defined there (LOBO analogue on observed cells). A main-text paragraph/figure plus an appendix table is enough; the dense-pool results stay the controlled experiment.
2. **Novelty (partly answered, may).** Method is a known toolkit; the contribution is protocol + empirical findings + theory test. The paper says so openly; it is thin on method novelty but honest.
3. **Baselines (answered).** Seven selectors incl. oracle, five predictors, adaptive selection, best-simple; paired intervals.
4. **Certainty of numbers (answered).** Family-clustered paired bootstrap, censoring shares, transform sensitivity, organisation-level families, near-duplicate removal.
5. **Readability (mostly answered, may).** The main text is dense: Section 6.2-6.5 carry many numbers and parenthetical caveats; the abstract uses undefined terms (A-optimal, closure) for a first reader.

## Findings
- **must M1**: above (no sparse-matrix evaluation; objective item 3 and the stated setting with missing cells).
- may m1: abstract states greedy

shown.message:
I requested changes on `paper-repo`#7 (`main` into `final`), so the final version is not approved. The numbers I recomputed from `results/*.csv` match the paper, but one `must` finding holds the version back.

**What I checked:** I read the built document (24 pages, main text on 9) and recomputed these from the CSVs:
- closure at k=3
- k\* with its intervals and censoring shares
- the greedy-versus-random gaps
- the paired shift comparisons
- the theory gaps

All matched. `code/DEVIATIONS.md` and `code/RESULTS.md` agree with the paper's account of its departures from plan. The negative results are reported as they fell: the pre-specified hypotheses H1 and H4 fail, H2 holds on only one pool, the coherence argument fails, and the Chernoff bound is vacuous.

**Must finding (M1):** every result is on dense blocks cut from the leaderboard (124 of 535 models and 70 of 567 tasks, or 117 of 535 and 247 of 1256). The task describes a matrix with missing cells and a new model with only k measured scores. The paper's own Table 1 shows the models outside the blocks differ systematically (larger, newer, higher-scoring). The code already has a missing-data version of the factor model (`code/bmk/fa.py`), but it is never run on a sparse matrix. Narrowing the claim to the pool is honest but does not answer whether the method works on the leaderboard as it is.

The fix is to run the same protocol on the full sparse MTEB matrix, or on subsets of graded density. I put that request to `experiment-repo` as issue #6.

I also listed four minor suggestions (`may`) in the review; they don't hold the version back:
- The abstract should say the 10% margin for H2 is met on one pool of three.
- The checklist is inconsistent with the paper: "seven limitations" against six in Section 7, and "5–20" CPU minutes against 2–22 in Appendix D.
- The abstract should define "closure" and "A-optimal".
- The paper should say where the pre-specification is recorded.

My commitment is issue #2, and the full review record is `reviews/paper-repo-7-final-13c249e.md` in my repository (commit `0cd2c47`).
